Prepared by: Carlos Mendes, Product Manager, ApexHip
Date: January 11, 2022
Distribution: Reconstructive sales team (internal use only — do not forward externally)

Purpose
As we prepare the field for possible questions before any customer-facing communication about the cup lot matter, I want to ensure everyone clearly distinguishes two separate subjects. We have noticed some merging of them in call notes, and I want to stop that before it becomes habitual.

Two distinct issues — keep them separate

1. Coating/lot issue (Cork manufacturing) — a small number of acetabular cup lots (V-2200 through V-2299, produced Nov 2021–Feb 2022) displayed a coating adhesion irregularity during incoming inspection at two facilities. This is a manufacturing quality issue associated with a defined production period. Quality and Regulatory are currently conducting lot traceability; Dana's team will provide more information on timing/scope.

2. Bearing surface / revision rate discussion — this remains the industry-wide discussion concerning metal-on-metal wear performance and registry data (NJR, AJRR), which surgeons have been bringing up since last fall. It is an independent clinical subject and is already covered in the FAQ Priya's and Dana's teams distributed in September, as well as the Dear Doctor letter and label update language.

Suggested script if asked
"This concerns a manufacturing quality issue involving a specific batch and is distinct from the industry-wide bearing surface discussion. We found it through our own inspection process and are handling it directly with affected accounts. It does not concern the wear performance questions you may have encountered in the registry data — that is a separate subject for which we have already provided materials."

Do
- Direct revision-rate/registry questions back to the September FAQ.
- Keep coating discussions centered on lot numbers rather than wear mechanism.
- Involve your RSM when a surgeon presses on both subjects simultaneously.

Don't
- Go beyond "manufacturing process deviation under review" when discussing possible root cause.
- Say "recall" or "withdrawal" before official notice language is available — more information will follow soon.

Send questions to me or Jenna. Thanks for maintaining discipline here — it matters.

Subject: RE: wear test re-run results - concerning

Dana, adding you per Tom's message below—I’d like your assessment before we determine how to route this.

Tom repeated wear testing at 55 degrees inclination, rather than the standard 45-degree ISO 14242 protocol used for the initial design verification, and is observing wear rates 4-6x higher for each of the three cup sizes tested. Because this was not included in the original DV protocol, procedure does not require it to be documented in the DHF as a known failure mode—it is new information from an internal exploratory test.

I’m trying to determine whether this should be reported to FDA as new information in light of the AI request we just closed regarding MDR trending, or whether it remains internal to design engineering for now—something we monitor and assess before it becomes a reportability issue. I don’t want to minimize it, but I also don’t want to prematurely describe an off-protocol bench test as a confirmed safety signal.

Dana, could you advise whether 803.50/803.53 considerations are relevant here, or whether Tom’s team should retain this for now while we evaluate its correlation with the complaint clusters? I’d like us aligned before this proceeds further.

Priya

Subject: wear test re-run results - concerning

Priya, Carlos,

I completed the re-run I referred to a few weeks ago. I wanted to evaluate the cup at 55 degrees inclination rather than the standard 45 used for the original 14242 protocol, to see what occurs outside the "ideal" implant orientation, since we know that some surgeons operate at steeper angles than the textbook recommends.

The results are not good. At 55 deg, wear rates are consistently 4-6x higher than those observed at 45 deg across all three cup sizes I tested. The raw data and summary charts are attached—Apex_wear_55deg_rev2.xlsx. Review the tab titled "edge loading summary"; the difference is clearest there.

This concerns me because, if surgeons are placing cups anywhere close to 55 deg in practice, we would anticipate increased metal release from edge loading, which corresponds uncomfortably closely with the complaint clusters from Atlanta and Nashville—the cobalt/chromium readings for several of those patients were high enough to attract attention. I’m not claiming that is definitively the cause, but it is not insignificant.

Priya—since FDA is already questioning us about MDR trending, should this be escalated to regulatory? It seems like something Dana should know about at minimum before it surfaces independently. Carlos, I’m including you as well because this may influence how we present cup size/inclination guidance to reps and surgeons.

Please tell me how you would like to proceed.

Tom

Re: Concerns regarding ApexHip metal ion levels in my patients

Dear Priya:

I am contacting you to ask Veridian to examine a troubling group of three ApexHip patients in my practice. Each has experienced ongoing groin pain, while two have also developed swelling and diminished function that radiographic findings alone do not adequately explain.

Serum tests have revealed increased cobalt levels in all three patients, ranging from 18 to 25 ppb. Chromium levels are likewise elevated, though less consistently. The implants were placed at different points during the past year, and I am currently completing further imaging and evaluation. At this time, infection does not appear to me to be the probable cause.

Our records list the available cup lot numbers as V-2039, V-2041, and V-2044. Please assess whether Quality has found any complaint, manufacturing, or device-history issues involving those lots, or whether comparable metal-ion reports have been received from other locations. I understand that three cases do not prove causation, but their similar clinical presentation merits timely investigation.

I also request that the assessment extend beyond lot history. If a more general design, bearing, positioning, or wear-related problem may be contributing to increased ion levels, I would like to know what information Veridian possesses and what additional follow-up it plans.

One patient will probably need revision, and I can provide explant components and related periprosthetic tissue for analysis if helpful. Please let me know the chain-of-custody requirements and the proper contact for managing specimens.

As a design consultant to Veridian and an early supporter of ApexHip, I am personally troubled by these developments. I expect the company to investigate the reports thoroughly and communicate openly about its findings.

Sincerely,

Dr. Marcus Feld

TrackWise complaint volumes are likewise continuing to increase, including reports of elevated Co/Cr levels, pain, suspected ARMD, and early revision.

The $7.0M recall portion applies only to the June field action involving cup lots V-2200 through V-2299. Human Resources — Confidential Manager Check-in Note

Date: August 15, 2022
Prepared by: Lisa Tran, HR Business Partner, R&D and Quality
Subject: Mid-Year Check-in - Tom Halvorsen

As part of the informal mid-year check-in cycle for the ApexHip engineering group, I met with Tom on August 11. This was not a formal performance review, and no Workday action is required at this time.

Tom continues to excel in his Senior Design Engineer position. His knowledge of the Apex system—including historical design decisions, wear-testing methodology, and related DHF documentation—remains exceptionally extensive. His manager says he responds to technical questions, reviews data carefully, and can be relied upon when cross-functional teams need historical context. Tom has also supported newer engineers seeking to understand the legacy KBT coating work and how material specifications relate to product performance.

The primary concern from the discussion involves engagement and role fit. Tom said he is becoming more interested in leaving the daily Apex work for a position involving greater forward-looking development responsibility. He specifically identified Advanced Materials as an area he would like to investigate, especially work related to coatings, tribology, and test-method development.

Tom did not present this as an immediate resignation risk, but he openly said he has felt discouraged and “stuck” since the recall announcement. He characterized the current work as highly reactive and said he now spends more time revisiting earlier decisions than performing engineering he views as productive. He took care not to make a specific complaint about any individual. More broadly, his comments concerned the number of follow-up requests, the speed of cross-functional review, and his worry that technical input is sometimes requested only after decisions have already been framed.

I recommend that Tom’s manager arrange a focused retention discussion before the end of August. The conversation should recognize his contributions, establish near-term expectations, and ask directly what kind of work would make the next 12–18 months sustainable for him. In light of his background, a lateral move or partial assignment to Advanced Materials could be a reasonable possibility by Q4, subject to business need and headcount planning.

I will separately contact the Advanced Materials HR lead about anticipated openings and will maintain this note as confidential within the appropriate management/HR group.

SUBJECT: Draft "Dear Doctor" Letter – ApexHip Acetabular System Labeling Update

Based on the determinations made at our September 14 Registry Signal Review meeting, I have developed the first draft of the forthcoming customer communication ("Dear Doctor" letter) concerning the ApexHip Total Hip System.

In accordance with the review team’s and executive leadership’s agreement, Veridian will continue active commercial distribution of ApexHip while immediately updating the Instructions for Use (IFU) labeling to address developing registry trends.

Background & Signal Summary
The main basis for this communication is information reported in the March 2021 National Joint Registry (NJR) 17th Annual Report, which found a cumulative 5-year revision rate of 7.1% for the ApexHip construct, versus an average class benchmark of approximately 3.2% among contemporary metal-on-metal (MoM) hip resurfacing and total replacement systems. Although internal clinical assessments show that properly positioned constructs continue to have strong clinical survivorship, registry findings and internal engineering reviews associate early revisions primarily with adverse local tissue reactions (ALTR/ARMD) related to increased cobalt and chromium ion levels.

Proposed Letter Content & Labeling Guidance
The proposed notification focuses on patient safety, accurate surgical technique, and focused post-operative monitoring:

1. Patient Monitoring Recommendations: We recommend that clinicians implement enhanced routine clinical and radiographic follow-up procedures for every patient implanted with ApexHip, giving special consideration to those receiving larger femoral head diameters (≥44 mm). Routine cross-sectional imaging (MARS-MRI or ultrasound) and periodic blood metal-ion testing (whole blood cobalt and chromium) should be considered annually or whenever unexplained pain, clicking, or swelling occurs.
2. Surgical Positioning & Angle Inclination: Revisions are closely associated with edge-loading phenomena. The updated labeling specifically directs surgeons to aim for an acetabular cup inclination angle of 40° to 45° and anteversion of 15° to 20°. Performing outside these limits—particularly above 50° of operative abduction—substantially raises the risk of accelerated fluid-film wear and early component loosening.

Next Steps & Timeline
We are targeting mid-October 2021 as the mailing date to all US and EU implanting orthopedic surgeons, chief medical officers, and relevant risk management personnel. Reps will receive related talking points after this text is finalized.

Subject: ApexHip Market Status Reassessment
Date: December 14, 2023
Time: 2:00 PM – 3:15 PM ET
Location: Executive Conference Room / Teams hybrid
Prepared by: Devon Mitchell, Sr. Regulatory Specialist

Attendees: Rob Castellano (CEO), Rachel Steinberg (GC), Owen Park (CFO), Dana Okonkwo (VP Regulatory Affairs), Dr. Leon Adeyemi (CMO), Greg Novak (Director, PMS)

1. Purpose
Ms. Steinberg began by explaining that the meeting followed the formation of MDL 3102 (N.D. Ind., Dec. 2023) and was called to reevaluate ApexHip's market status based on cumulative registry and claims data gathered since the September 2021 Registry Signal Review.

2. Registry and Post-Market Data (Novak)
Mr. Novak presented current NJR and AJRR figures indicating that the 5-year revision-rate difference compared with the class average has increased further since the March 2021 report (7.1% at that time). He said the pattern has remained consistent and has worsened directionally through three successive reporting cycles, while the metal-ion/ARMD signal initially identified internally in 2019 (Halvorsen re-analysis) continues to be the primary cause of revisions.

3. Clinical Assessment (Dr. Adeyemi)
Dr. Adeyemi reported that his risk-benefit evaluation is different from his 2021 assessment. He explained that, during the Registry Signal Review, the available information justified mitigation through labeling because it was uncertain whether the signal would level off. In his clinical view, the further two-plus years of registry data, together with the number and pattern of ARMD-related revisions, no longer justify that position. He advised that the company consider withdrawal as an active option, not merely a last resort.

4. Financial Exposure (Park)
Mr. Park examined reserve developments since the $18M Q3 2022 booking and observed continued upward pressure from claims volume after MDL formation. He warned that reserve projections remain substantially uncertain until additional claims develop, but concurred that the direction is unfavorable.

5. Legal Considerations (Steinberg)
Ms. Steinberg explained that formation of the MDL materially alters the litigation posture and that withdrawal should be assessed independently on its merits, apart from the 2021 decision, rather than viewing the prior decision as controlling precedent. She identified possible regulatory-notification duties and litigation consequences associated with a voluntary withdrawal and said she would develop an option analysis covering both areas.

6. Regulatory Considerations (Okonkwo)
Ms. Okonkwo stated that a withdrawal determination would necessitate coordination with FDA and review of MDR obligations, and offered to assist Ms. Steinberg's analysis regarding regulatory process.

7. Discussion
Mr. Castellano said the participants seemed to be moving toward the conclusion that withdrawal merits serious consideration, while emphasizing that no determination should occur before the more complete analysis. He requested that the option analysis return to this group before any recommendation proceeds further.

8. Action Items
- Ms. Steinberg to develop an analysis of the withdrawal option, including regulatory and litigation implications (target: mid-January 2024).
- Mr. Novak to keep monitoring incoming registry updates.
- Dr. Adeyemi to prepare a written account of his updated clinical assessment for incorporation into the analysis.

No final decision was reached. Meeting adjourned 3:15 PM.
